items.title: I'm making LLMs work on small and old devices
items.content:
Run the biggest language model you can on the smallest hardware you own.

TV boxes, old tablets, single-board computers and routers all have a CPU, some RAM and flash storage that sit idle most of the day. smolmaxxing finds the biggest model each of them can really run, then pushes it further with custom kernels, careful memory use and weights streamed from flash. Every number in this repo was measured on the device itself.

Both devices run 8B and 16B mixture-of-experts models on about 1 GB of RAM by keeping only part of each model in memory and reading the rest from flash as it's needed.

More devices (phones, single-board computers, routers) are coming. The techniques aren't tied to one box: the 1-bit kernel needs only basic NEON, and the flash streaming works on any Linux or Android device with more model than RAM.

All of it is a patch on llama.cpp . The main ideas:

Kernels built for the chip. A 1-bit lookup-table kernel, repacked 2-bit and ternary formats for the Cortex-A55, and versions of them for the A7, which has no dot-product instructions.

Less RAM per model. Most of a small model's vocabulary is rarely used, so we drop those output rows. On the TV, a "headless" mode also stops the launcher and Google services while a model runs.

Experts paged from flash. A mixture-of-experts model only uses a few experts per token. We keep the popular ones in RAM, read the others from flash on demand and prefetch the next layer's. This is how 8B and 16B models run on 1 GB.

Streaming for dense models bigger than RAM, at the flash's full speed.

docs/how-it-works.md has every technique with its measured gain.

The quickest start is a ready-made model file from Hugging Face. They need the patched llama.cpp: stock llama.cpp can't load them.

TV box or another ARMv8.2 Android device: docs/tv-box-setup.md

Jailbroken iPad on iOS 12: ipad-air/README.md

All model files and how to rebuild them: docs/models.md

every chat benchmark ( results.jsonl ) and the raw logs

the first experiment: a 260K-parameter story model

MIT . The llama.cpp patches are derivatives of llama.cpp (MIT). Model weights keep their own licenses, and the evaluation texts are Wikipedia excerpts (CC BY-SA 4.0).

Built on llama.cpp and llama2.c . Models from Qwen , unsloth (GGUFs and importance matrices), PrismML (Bonsai), inclusionAI (Ling-mini-2.0), tablinum (Moon-Beam), bartowski and mradermacher (GGUFs), Google (Gemma) and stories260K . The iPad is jailbroken with Amethyst . The banner uses Archivo (SIL OFL) and is rendered by tools/banner/render.sh . The 🤏 logo is the pinching-hand emoji from Google's Noto Emoji (Apache 2.0).

items.title: Hijacking Samsung TV Smart Hub Ads
items.summary: networking, reversing
items.content:
I have a Samsung smart TV from 2022. At some point, the Smart Hub started

displaying ads. I think it’s absolutely disgusting that a device that I paid

for and own, and that doesn’t use any additional Samsung “free” services is

forcing ads on me, just to generate additional revenue for Samsung from an

already-sold device. I was blocking the ads via my Pi-hole

instance, until I was tinkering with my homelab and networking setup not

that long ago and broke something. That caused the ads to start appearing

again, which reminded me of their existence.

Around the same time, the eMudhra CA certificate fiasco

took place, and the “compromised” private key was added to

mitmproxy . mitmproxy is an open-source project for inspecting,

replaying and modifying HTTP(S) network traffic. Normally, in order for it to

be able to intercept TLS-encrypted traffic, the “victim” device must trust a

custom certificate created by mitmproxy - this way mitmproxy can decrypt

the traffic, inspect it, and then re-encrypt it using a real certificate before

forwarding it to the intended destination. Unfortunately, some devices don’t

allow adding custom SSL certificates to their truststore - like my Samsung TV.

Intercepting TV traffic with mitmproxy Mikrotik configuration (adapt to your router as needed)

# 192.168.0.7 is my raspberry-pi with mitmproxy

add dst-address=0.0.0.0/0 gateway=192.168.0.7 routing-table=tv-proxy

add src-address=192.168.0.9/32 action=lookup-only-in-table table=tv-proxy

add chain=forward action=accept src-address=192.168.0.9 connection-state=established,related

add chain=forward action=accept dst-address=192.168.0.9 connection-state=established,related

sudo iptables -I FORWARD 1 -s 192.168.0.9 -j ACCEPT

sudo iptables -I FORWARD 1 -d 192.168.0.9 -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT

sudo iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -i eth0 -s 192.168.0.9 -p tcp --dport 80 -j REDIRECT --to-port 8080

sudo iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -i eth0 -s 192.168.0.9 -p tcp --dport 443 -j REDIRECT --to-port 8080

sudo iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 192.168.0.9/32 -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE

uvx --from mitmproxy mitmweb --web-port 8083 -p 8081 --emudhra --ssl-insecure --mode transparent --set stream_large_bodies = 1m

With the eMudhra certificate being exposed, anyone can now create a custom

SSL certificate for an arbitrary domain (let’s say a Samsung ad network

domain), sign it with the compromised CA certificate, and all devices that have

the eMudhra CA certificate in their truststores will trust the custom SSL

certificate. This is why software vendors were racing (some more, some less) to

revoke the certificate from their truststores, so that browsers, computers and

smart phones wouldn’t be susceptible to this kind of attack. Luckily for me,

Samsung did not yet release an update for my TV that would revoke the

certificate. This allowed me to route all traffic from the TV through

mitmproxy and get a list of all the domains and endpoints that my TV talks

to, but also see the structure of the requests and response payloads.

Turns out the flow is pretty simple: when something interesting happens on the

TV, the TV sends a request to https://catalyst.adgrx.com/adopportunity with

some details about the TV. When you return to the Smart Hub, the “home screen”

of the TV, so to speak, the TV sends requests to

https://tvx.adgrx.com/impressions/tile again with some details about the TV,

and in response it receives either an empty JSON object ( {} ) or a JSON

response describing an ad to display at the top of the Smart Hub.

So I wrote a simple server in Rust that handles the same /impressions/tile

endpoint and always returns JSON with an ad, except instead of links to an

actual ad image, it has a link to a random photo of my family. I also included

a simple frontend where I can manage the images that should be served.

Additionally, the server blackholes any other *.adgrx.com request and returns

Seems like every day a new security issue crops up at Instagram.

New Instagram AI Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-126361 📢 Source: GitHub_M 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False Astro is a web framework for content-driven websites. Prior to 7.4.5, Astro rendered a string used as a dynamic element name as raw HTML after applying an incomplete character filter. A / in the string could make an HTML parser treat the remainder as attributes, allowing untrusted element-name input to inject event-handler markup. The .astro dynamic-tag renderer, JSX renderer, and MDX renderer were affected, and exploitation required an application to use request-controlled or stored untrusted data as all or part of an element name. This issue is fixed in version 7.4.5. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-12T22:26:35.206Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-126361

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: Agent Name Service is Now Part of The Linux Foundation
items.content:
Agent Name Service (ANS) now has a home at the Linux Foundation . The launch happened at KubeCon North America in Salt Lake City, and you might remember that the foundation first announced its plans for the project way back in June.

GoDaddy, Cloudflare, Salesforce, and DigiCert are among the organizations now involved with ANS, bringing the total number up to eleven.

One of the early deployments of ANS has been in AGNTCY , another project under the foundation, where its directory of AI agents can now check an agent’s ANS identity.

Announcing the move, Jim Zemlin, CEO of the Linux Foundation, had this to share:

Autonomous AI agents are transacting and operating across global systems, but they can't succeed without verifiable identity.

Under the neutral governance of the Linux Foundation, ANS provides a common foundation for trust that the entire industry can adopt, implement and improve together.

Platforms identify AI agents in their own ways, and a service that receives a request from one has no standardized way to confirm who the agent represents.

ANS tackles this by linking each agent to a domain name its operator owns, the same way a website is tied to its domain. Each version of an agent gets its own name, such as ans://v1.4.2.travel.example.com .

To register an agent, the operator first has to prove it controls that domain. Certificates are then issued for the agent, and every registration goes into a public log that anyone can read.

ANS also publishes details about each agent in DNS , the internet's address book, and other systems can then look them up with tools they already use.

The main DNS records use a format from a separate project called DNS-AID . ANS adds one record of its own that points to the agent's entry in the public log.

When an agent sends a request, the receiving system can check that its registration exists, that it has not been revoked, and that the agent really holds the key tied to it.

ANS only covers who the agent is. Deciding what it can do is left to the receiving system, and platforms have to add the check themselves.

A technical steering committee now oversees the project . It starts with five seats, held by three people from GoDaddy , Ken Huang of DistributedApps.ai , and Michael Kantor of Hashgraph Online (HOL).

That lineup is only a starting point. The first election has to be held within 12 months, and after it, the charter prevents any one company from holding half or more of the seats ( to ensure vendor neutrality , I assume ).

The charter also mentions that meetings are meant to be open to the public and that discussions and decisions should be visible to everyone.

As for all the code in the project, the Go, Rust, and Java libraries currently use the MIT license, but new code contributed from now on has to use the Apache 2.0 license.

ANS began in 2025 as a draft sent to the IETF , the internet standards body, and a follow-up came in October. Drafts like these have no formal standing at the IETF and are not endorsed by it.

At present, the Linux Foundation calls the specification formalized. The reference code and a local demo are on the project's GitHub page , and the specifications are on ansinfo.ai .
